I'll start by assessing the current state of the project.
I've read through the packet. Here's where things stand.

**The project:** a single-user notebook — one continuous chronological stream of writing, tagged retrospectively with subjects rather than split into per-project notebooks, plus TODOs, pinned lists, an events calendar, and document collections. Mac and Android, plain durable files, built solo in the evenings. It was extracted from Portal when the notebook turned out to be where ~90% of the value was.

**Where the work is:** problem clarification is essentially complete — problem, precedent, stakeholders, requirements, and five open questions are all written and current. Nothing has been built and no decisions are recorded yet, which is correct. `solution/` and `failures/` are empty.

Three things worth flagging before we pick a direction:

**1. The goal documents were never confirmed with you.** The previous session wrote problem.md, requirements.md, stakeholders.md, and summary.md but the alignment check at the end of problem clarification didn't happen. Everything downstream rests on those, so it's worth ten minutes now rather than discovering a mismatch after a prototype.

**2. The agreed next step was a prototype, not solution design.** Q1 (can one surface be vim-compatible *and* render equations/figures/tables inline?) and Q4 (what stack, given OS integration is a real cost?) gate essentially everything else, and the plan was to answer both with one spike: the smallest thing with a real vim mode, an inline equation, an inline image, and a table — typed into at full speed, plus **printing a range and pasting an image**, since Tauri is where you've actually *measured* pain rather than suspected it.

**3. One thing in Q4 has never been put to you directly.** The previous session added a fourth candidate — building this as an extension to an existing editor (VSCode, à la Foam/Dendron) — for honest pricing, but you've never reacted to it. It's close to your current working setup, it gets vim, typing performance, printing and file handling for free, and it fails R1.5 ("the UX is the user's own") while covering no mobile at all. It deserves an explicit yes or no from you rather than sitting in a document.

So: **start with the alignment check on the goal docs, then move into the Q1/Q4 prototype?** Or if you'd rather go straight at Q4 option 4 as a conversation first — it could shrink or reshape the prototype considerably — that's a reasonable reordering.

Hello! We’re starting a new Clarity session. As you assess the current state of the project, you can start by reading .clarity-protocol/handoff.md — this was a handoff document prepared specifically for you by the previous Clarity instance. The rest of the clarity protocol, and the files in notes/, will also be directly relevant. Take a look at them and see where we are.

I'll start by reading the handoff document and getting oriented.
I've read the handoff, the full goal packet, `notes.md`, `carried-over.md`, and your `01 general ideas.md`. Here's where we are.

## The state

Problem clarification is essentially done. `problem.md`, `precedent.md`, `stakeholders.md`, `requirements.md`, and five open questions are all written and internally consistent. `decisions/`, `solution/`, and `failures/` are empty — correctly, since nothing has been decided that needed deciding. Nothing has been built.

One gap: **step 11, verifying alignment with you, never happened.** The goal documents were written but never confirmed. Everything downstream rests on them, so let me put the spine in front of you rather than ask permission to do so.

## What the documents claim, compressed — accept or correct

**The problem** is not "I need a notes app." It's that you think by writing, and there's currently no place to do it that is simultaneously always available, pleasant enough to sustain, and organized enough to find things in later. Twenty years of evidence say the binding constraints have always been *availability*, *fit*, and *findability* — and never features. Era 2 (paper, four status symbols, a calendar section) outperformed Era 3 (Docs/M365, strictly more features) decisively.

**The consequence** — and this is the sharpest claim in the packet — is that the target is *smaller* than "a high-powered notebook app," and the design should be suspicious of anything not serving those three. That's a real constraint and it will bite later; worth agreeing to it now or rejecting it now.

**The structural idea** is subjects-as-tags-on-ranges rather than notebooks-as-containers. Capture stops having a routing decision, "move a range between notebooks" evaporates, overlap becomes free. In exchange, search and filtering move from nice-to-have to load-bearing: a single undifferentiated stream with weak filtering is worse than several small notebooks.

**The primary requirement is experience, not capability** — 130 WPM with no perceptible latency, no state ever at risk, tunable excellent typography, vim compatibility, and "the UX is mine." These are stated as hard requirements with the same standing as functional ones, on the grounds that Era 3 died of exactly this.

**The forced-review discovery**: your filling two-page spread was an accidental garbage collector — anything not worth transcribing died by decision rather than neglect. Digital lists never fill. The packet defers the mechanism but commits now to recording a last-touched timestamp on every TODO from day one, because no staleness mechanism can be retrofitted without it.

If any of that is wrong or off-emphasis, this is the cheap moment to say so.

## Three things to flag

**1. The agreed next step is a prototype, not solution design.** Q1 (can one surface be vim-compatible *and* render equations, figures, tables inline?) and Q4 (what stack?) gate nearly everything. The plan was one spike answering both: smallest thing with a real vim mode, an inline equation, an inline image, and a table — typed into at full speed — plus **printing a range and pasting an image**, because Tauri is where you've *measured* pain rather than suspected it.

**2. Q4 option 4 has never actually been put to you.** The previous session added "build it as a VSCode extension" to the option list for honest pricing, but you never reacted. It gets vim, typing performance, file handling, and printing for free; it's close to your current setup; Foam and Dendron are precedents. It costs R1.5 — the UX would emphatically not be yours — and covers no mobile at all. It deserves an explicit yes or no rather than sitting in a document quietly not being chosen.

**3. The name.** "Notebook" is a placeholder and the directory follows it. Trivial now, annoying later.

Confirm or correct the spine above, then settle Q4 option 4 in conversation — because if it survives, it reshapes the prototype substantially, and if it dies, killing it explicitly is worth doing before we spend evenings on a spike. Then build the Q1/Q4 spike.

Where would you like to start?

The compressed claims: Agree with all of them, but I’ll note that “smaller than a high-powered notebook app” is a fairly vague statement — we’ll need to make it more concrete. But I agree that we should really focus on “joyful user experience” and build outwards from that, rather than starting from some kind of feature maximalism.

Prototyping as a next step is a good idea, but we should sketch out just what we want to prototype before we start on that.

# Decisions

## D1: This is not built as an extension to an existing editor

**Date:** 2026-08-12
**Status:** decided
**Resolves:** Q4, option 4

**Decision.** The project will not be built as a VSCode (or other editor) extension, in the manner of Foam or Dendron. The remaining Q4 candidates are the three that ship an application: fully native, native shell with a web view for the editor surface, and full web shell.

**Why.** The option was attractive on paper — vim mode, typing performance, file handling and printing all free — and it is close to the current working setup. It dies on **mobile**, and on measured rather than suspected grounds: the user has been running this exact arrangement as a stopgap, and reports that the total absence of mobile access "has been a huge practical blocker in every VSCode-based project I've done lately." That is Era 2's failure mode reproduced deliberately: a system that works well and is in the wrong place. Availability wherever thinking happens (R24) is the requirement the entire project exists to satisfy, and no amount of desktop quality buys it back. The secondary cost — R1.5, "the UX is the user's own" — would have been arguable on its own; the mobile gap is not.

**What the option leaves behind, which is more valuable than the option was.** Running VSCode-with-vim-plugins as a stopgap produced firsthand evidence that survives the decision:

- **The typing experience is pleasant at 130 WPM.** VSCode is Electron. R1.1 (latency), R1.4 (vim) and R1.3 (rendering quality) are therefore *jointly satisfiable in a web-based stack* — an existence proof, not an argument. This raises the prior on Q4 candidates 2 and 3 considerably.
- **The visual experience was made very good by custom themes the user wrote themselves.** This is direct evidence about what "joyful" means in practice for this user — a large fraction of it is typography and colour, it is achievable in web tech, and the user has already done the design work once. Those themes are a concrete partial specification of R1.3 and should be treated as an input, not re-derived.

**Consequences.**
- Q4 narrows to three candidates, all of which ship an application on both platforms.
- The Tauri finding (OS integration is painful) is now the *only* remaining negative evidence in Q4, and it is about Tauri's OS bridge specifically, not about web rendering. The prototype must therefore aim squarely at the OS-integration boundary — printing and image paste — rather than at rendering quality, which is no longer in doubt.
- The existing custom VSCode themes should be retrieved and used as a starting point for the notebook's typography and colour, and as a benchmark the prototype has to match.

**What would reopen this.** Only the mobile requirement being dropped, which would mean abandoning the fix for Era 2's failure. Effectively: nothing.

content:
Four good threads. Let me take them in reverse order of how much thinking they need — starting with the one that's already settled.
## Q4.4 is dead, and it left something behind

Recorded as **D1**. The mobile gap kills it — and on measured grounds, which is the strongest kind here: you've been *running* the arrangement and found the absence of mobile blocking in practice. That's Era 2's failure mode reproduced on purpose. R1.5 alone would have been arguable; this isn't.

But the more useful half is what the stopgap proved. You find VSCode-with-vim *pleasant* at 130 WPM, and VSCode is Electron. So R1.1, R1.3 and R1.4 are jointly satisfiable in web tech — that's an existence proof, not an argument, and it retires the rendering worry entirely. **Q4 is now purely a question about the OS-integration boundary**, which means the spike should aim at printing and paste and can stop trying to prove that text can look good.

Second: you got there by **writing custom themes**. That's the most concrete thing anyone has said about what "joyful" means for you — a large fraction of it is typography and colour, you've already done the design work once, and it's portable. Those themes should be an *input* to this project and a benchmark the prototype has to match, not something we re-derive from first principles. I've flagged retrieving them. Do you still have them?

## Making "smaller" concrete

You're right that it's vague, and vague scope discipline reliably loses to a concrete feature. Here's a rule that isn't vague, and that comes out of your own evidence rather than out of taste:

**v1 is Era 2, plus the fixes for the three eras' failures. Nothing else.**

That expands to a closed list:

| Source | What it buys |
|---|---|
| Era 2's successes | The continuous stream; a TODO list with four statuses; a calendar section |
| Era 1's failure | Search |
| Era 2's failure | Mac and Android |
| Era 3's failure | Joy — latency, typography, vim — and structure: equations, tables, inline figures |

Plus one item no era had: **subjects-as-tags**, which earns its place because it's the mechanism that makes findability work in a single undifferentiated stream. Without it, search alone probably isn't enough, and the whole "one stream, not N notebooks" bet fails.

Everything else in the requirements — branching, filesets, URL snapshotting, the browser extension, pinned lists, dynamic TODO groupings, due-date urgency ranking — is **Era-2-plus**, and each one has to answer a specific question to get in: *what does having this here beat?* Filesets currently compete with a folder and a text file. The browser extension competes with copy-paste. That's a fair fight and some of them will win it — but they win it later, on evidence, and not by being on the original list.

The virtue of this rule is that it's falsifiable and traceable. When something wants in, we don't argue about whether the app is getting "too big"; we ask which era's failure it fixes, or what it beats.

Two things I'd flag as genuinely arguable, because I think you'll want to fight about them:

- **The events calendar is in** by this rule (Era 2 had one, it worked) even though it looks like a satellite. I think that's correct and slightly surprising.
- **Due-date urgency ranking (R16) is out** by this rule, since Era 2's due dates are what *failed* at scale. But R16 is specifically the fix for that failure, so it arguably qualifies as an Era-2-failure fix. I lean toward in — but the last-touched timestamp goes in regardless, since that's the irreversible part.

Does this rule do the work you wanted? If so I'll write it up as a scope document and we can settle the boundary cases against it.

## The name

Working through the list by fit rather than by sound alone — several are beautiful and mean the wrong thing, which matters for something you'll live inside for twenty years.

**Actively wrong:** *apophenia* and *pareidolia* both name the perception of pattern that isn't there — the failure mode of a thinking tool, not its function. *Asphodel* is the meadow where the ordinary dead go; naming the graveyard problem after itself is a poor omen. *Labyrinth* is a place designed to prevent you finding things.

**Beautiful, no fit:** *petrichor*, *oneiric*, *liminal*, *ember*, *epode*. I'd also gently set aside *nepantla* — Anzaldúa's term carries specific weight that a personal notes app probably shouldn't borrow.

**The real candidates**, all of which mean something true about this thing:

- **tephra** — volcanic ash fall. Tephrochronology is the practice of dating strata *by their ash layers*: a continuous accumulation of deposited fragments, readable in order, datable by where it sits. That is precisely the data model — a chronological stream you date by position. Six letters, unclaimed, types fast, works as a command and a directory.
- **clepsydra** — a water clock: a timekeeper that works because **a finite vessel fills**. That's Q3, named. Gorgeous and eerily apt, but long and hard to spell at speed.
- **paredra** — one who sits beside; a divine assessor. The tool as the thing at your elbow while you think. Lovely and unclaimed.
- **nautilus** — grows by sealing off each outgrown chamber and moving on, *keeping every one*, in order, forming the spiral. Almost too apt. But it's GNOME's file manager and broadly spoken for.
- **parallax** — true position determined by viewing from two angles; a physicist's word, and two devices onto one object. Slightly claimed.

**My pick is tephra**, on the grounds that it means the thing exactly, it's short enough to type without thinking, and nobody owns it. *Clepsydra* is the more beautiful word and the deeper joke; *paredra* is the warmest.

Your call — and it's genuinely cheap right now.

The VSCode themes shouldn’t be an input to this, because I designed those for the experience of coding in particular — I have very different visual ideas in mind for this app! In fact, I want to do something closer to the visual styling I designed for the Clarity app.

On the events calendar: That was actually a success in era *3*, not 2 — I did it using an Excel spreadsheet, which despite the general awfulness of Excel was good enough. In this version, the simplest version of that calendar would be one particular file that I keep pinned — so if we have the ability to have a range of files (for lists, etc) then a v1 events calendar could just be a special case of that.

For due-date urgency ranking, I think that I’d want to get that in as a relatively early part of TODO design. But I think we can discuss where we want to stage the TODO feature within the design overall. (Really, I think we should try to break this design into major components and sequence them — a good part of solution design)

For the naming, “paredra” was my initial favorite but I think it creates too much of a risk of anthromorphization, which is not the vibe I want for this — this is by its nature a *tool*, not a companion. I have a paredra, I’m married to her. So I think “tephra” is a good name. Let’s go with that — in a moment I’ll rename this directory and the corresponding git repo, too.

That principle is now a constraint on the whole design surface — interface copy, any assistive or generative feature, error messages, and anything that might otherwise acquire a persona. Tephra is a substance, which is the correct register.

# Scope

The concrete answer to "smaller than a high-powered notebook app." It is a counting rule, and it is countable — which is what makes it usable in an argument.

## The rule

**Tephra is a small number of view types over one directory of plain files.** The scope number is the count of *view types*, not the count of features. This falls out of R26 (plain durable formats) rather than being imposed on top of it, and it makes the departer's exit structural: if every artifact is already a file another program can open, "leaving" is not an export feature, it is stopping.

## The types

Three native types, each with its own UX. Everything else in the directory is either **external** (PDFs and other documents, opened by the OS) or **embedded** (PNGs and images, referenced from markdown and rendered inline).

| Type | UX |
|---|---|
| **Markdown** (`.md`) | The reading and editing surface. The notebook stream, branched documents, and pinned lists are all this type. Possible later export to docx and similar. |
| **TODO** | Seen *only* through the TODO experience — urgency ranking, statuses, due dates. Never edited as raw text in normal use. |
| **Fileset** | A directory with a master index. Browse, open individually or en masse, annotate, snapshot. |

Pinned lists (R18) and the events calendar (R19) are markdown files, not types. That is the test working: they dissolved into an existing type rather than adding one.

**Type is declared by name, not inferred.** Portal found the failure this prevents: a mutable list mistyped as append-only notebook content merges with append-union semantics and *silently duplicates edited lines* — no error, the file quietly fills with near-duplicate paragraphs. Explicit typing is what makes merge safe.

**Open: whether three types means three syntaxes.** The alternative is one syntax family — markdown, leniently parsed — with three declared types over it, so that a TODO file remains sensible to a plain reader even though it is only ever *seen* through the TODO UX. That costs the TODO UX some freedom and buys a structural exit, one parser and one merge story, and a v3 that can open the hand-edited TODO file v1 left behind. Undecided.

**Open: whether the subject view is a fourth type.** A subject view is a filtered assembly of ranges from many markdown files, and it is the view that tests the central bet of the design. Read-only, it folds into the markdown UX and the count stays at three. *Editable*, it is a composite surface writing back into source ranges — the most technically demanding thing in the design, and absent from the count above.

## What gets in, and when

The admission test is: **what does having this here beat?** Filesets compete with a folder and a text file; a browser extension competes with copy-paste. Some will win that fight, but they win it later and on evidence from use.

Which reframes the last stage of the sequencing (`solution/components.md`): **v3 is not "add the remaining features," it is "promote the ones that earned it."** v1 already ships a TODO list — a pinned markdown file with checkboxes — and a fileset — a directory with a notes file. v1 should deliberately *run* those plain versions rather than doing without, so that promotion happens against a specific recorded failure rather than an argument.

## The rule that decides what may be deferred

**Data cannot be backfilled; mechanisms can be deferred.** Deferring the TODO *UX* to v3 is free. Deferring the last-touched *timestamp* is not, because every existing item then looks equally fresh. Dates are the same class — file mtime does not survive sync, copy, or git, so a date not written into the filename or frontmatter is retroactively unreconstructible. So is subject-tag syntax, which v1 decides implicitly whether or not v1 has tagging.

Every v1 decision gets checked against: *if this is built in v3, will the corpus from v1 and v2 support it?*

# Components and sequencing

The decomposition of the build, and the order. Read with `goal/scope.md`, which supplies the counting rule and the deferral rule this ordering rests on.

## Components

1. **Format** — markdown plus extensions; how dates, subjects, bookmarks and TODO fields are represented in plain text.
2. **Editing surface** — vim mode, raw/rendered switching, inline widgets (Q1).
3. **Visual system** — typography, colour, spacing (R1.3). Reference is the Clarity app's styling.
4. **Storage and sync** — offline operation, two devices, reconciliation (Q2).
5. **Retrieval** — search, subject views, bookmarks.
6. **Range operations** — select, then tag / branch / print / bookmark.
7. **Structured lists** — TODO with urgency ranking; pinned lists.
8. **Filesets** — collections, snapshotting, browser extension.
9. **Mobile** — possibly a separate stack entirely (Q5).
10. **OS integration** — printing, paste, open-with, drag-and-drop.

Two are expensive to change later and everything else is comparatively cheap to reorder: **the format**, because it is the durable contract, the thing both platforms share, and what any merge must operate on; and **the editing surface plus visual system**, because they decide whether the thing gets used at all.

## Sequencing

**v1 — single-device Mac, the stream, excellent editing.** No sync layer, no mobile, no TODO or fileset UX. Synced by hand if at all. This is already the default place the writing happens, and it starts accumulating the corpus that makes everything downstream testable rather than theoretical.

**v2 — sync, then Android.** The purpose is road miles on the problem the project exists for: doing this from many places.

**v3 — promote what earned it.** TODO, filesets, and the rest, admitted against recorded failures of their plain-file stand-ins.

## What each stage must prove, and the constraints that carry backwards

**v1's UX is the stream, not a file list.** "N markdown files" describes storage; R6 asks for one continuous chronological stream. A folder-of-notes navigator is a different product and leaves the central bet untested.

**The stream is stored as day files and edited as one surface, and reconciling those is v1's hardest problem.** Day files give durable dates and make merge tractable — append-union works precisely because each day file is append-only. But an editor component edits *one* document. The options are stitching a window of day files into a single document with per-region write-back, stacking per-day editor instances, or storing coarser and accepting worse merge granularity. Portal never faced this because it delegated editing outward; Tephra cannot. **This belongs in the prototype spec**, alongside Q1's vim-plus-inline-rendering question and Q4's printing and image-paste questions.

**v1 makes two format decisions it cannot revisit**: where the date lives (filename or frontmatter — not mtime, which does not survive sync, copy or git), and the subject-tag syntax, which v1 fixes implicitly whether or not v1 has tagging. Search is nearly free over a directory of markdown and fixes Era 1's failure, so it belongs in v1 too.

**v2 bundles two new risks and should unbundle them.** Sync and a second platform are both new and both risky; if v2 feels bad it will not be obvious which one is wrong. Sync must come first regardless, since the phone needs a corpus for any judgement about it to mean anything — so the only question is whether to live on sync alone for some weeks before starting Android. Doing so means the phone lands on a substrate already trusted.

**The uncomfortable part of this ordering is that mobile — the requirement the project exists for — lands late.** That is survivable because Era 2 worked excellently for years without it; the access failure came from a change in circumstances, not from day one. But it is the place this sequencing could be badly wrong, and it deserves re-examination rather than a shrug. The specific risk to watch: **v1's editor choice may not port to Android, and that only becomes visible in v2.** The v1 stack decision should therefore be made with an explicit answer to "does this editing surface exist on Android, and if not, am I willing to build it twice?" — which the requirements permit, but only deliberately.

**Deferral is safe only where what is deferred is a mechanism over data already being recorded.** See `goal/scope.md`.

I read the Portal notebook design alongside your note — it turns out to have already hit one of the questions your framing raises, and to have left another one open that Tephra can't dodge. Let me lay out where I agree and the four places I'd push.

## The three types: agree, but it bundles two things worth separating

Your framing is right and it's a real sharpening — three UXes is a countable scope number in a way "small number of views" wasn't. But "native file type" bundles *type* (how a file is named, parsed, merged) with *syntax* (what's actually in the bytes), and those can be split.

Portal found a genuine bug here worth inheriting: a mutable side list that got typed as an append-only notebook file merged with append-union semantics, which **silently duplicates edited lines** — no error, the file just quietly fills with near-duplicate paragraphs. The lesson is that types must be **explicit and declared by name**, not inferred from extension or context.

But that argues for three declared types, not three syntaxes. I'd propose: **one syntax family — markdown, leniently parsed — with three declared types over it.** The TODO file is markdown that a plain reader finds sensible, even though you only ever *see* it through the TODO UX. That costs the TODO UX some freedom (it has to round-trip a markdown document, not a bespoke format) and buys three things: the exit stays structural rather than aspirational, there's one parser and one merge story instead of three, and — the sequencing argument, which I find the most persuasive — **v1 has no TODO UX, so during v1 and v2 your TODO list simply *is* a hand-edited markdown file.** If v3's TODO type is markdown-shaped, v3 opens that file. If it's a distinct syntax, you migrate.

**The one thing missing from the count of three:** the subject/search view. A subject view is a filtered assembly of ranges from many .md files, and it's the view that tests the central bet of the whole design. If it's read-only, it folds into the .md UX and the count stays at three. If it's *editable*, it's a composite surface writing back into source ranges — which is the most technically demanding thing in the design and it doesn't appear anywhere in the type list. Worth deciding deliberately rather than discovering.

## "Cache" is the wrong word, and the difference is a data-loss bug

I agree with the substance — local directories over a network source of truth — but the word matters here, because caches have a specific safety property: **a cache may be discarded and refilled from truth.** That's exactly false for this. Between writing on the plane and pushing on landing, the local copy is *the only copy*. The correct name is a **local replica with write-back**, and the distinction is load-bearing the first time something goes wrong and some recovery path thinks "just refill from the server."

Except — and this is where your instinct is exactly right — **for attachments.** Twenty years of markdown is a few hundred megabytes; twenty years of PDFs and pasted images is not, and the phone will feel that first. So there are two disciplines in one directory: **text is a replica** (never evictable until pushed), **blobs are a genuine cache** (evictable, refetchable from truth). That's a real design consequence, and it means the phone can hold the whole corpus of *thinking* without holding the whole corpus of *material*.

Two other things your statement decides that are worth making explicit:

- **It's a topology decision, not a reconciliation decision.** A star with a hub eliminates peer-to-peer and local-network-only sync. It buys a canonical history, a backup for free, and a phone that syncs without the Mac being awake. It costs a hub you must keep working for twenty years — and one that holds other people's information, which is a stated constraint in the requirements and bears on *where* that hub lives. ## The notebook is one document

**The app exposes a single logical document.** Conceptually the notebook is one enormous markdown file; the split into day files exists only because very large files become unwieldy. Everything above the storage layer — editor, search, range operations, addressing — sees one continuous stream.

## D10: Navigation is a list of sections; the default section is the pins

**Date:** 2026-08-12
**Status:** decided

**Decision.** The left nav is a list of **sections**, each an expando, each one a fileset. Expanding shows its entries; clicking an entry goes to it, in the current window or a new one. An entry is one of four things: a **bookmark** (jump to a place in a file), a **file** (jump to its start), a **URL** (open in the browser), or a **document Tephra does not handle**, such as a PDF (open by OS intent). **The default section always exists** and holds the pinned items at the top.

**Why this beats "pinning is a property."** Both were on the table. Membership in a distinguished fileset wins on two counts. It is **one file to read** rather than a flag scattered across the corpus that must be discovered by scan — and it therefore has an **explicit order**, which a scan-derived pin list does not, and which a navigation panel needs. The earlier objection that the events calendar is a table rather than a collection of pointers dissolves: the calendar is a *file entry within* a section, not a section.

**Consequence for sequencing.** Filesets acquire the **navigation** role from v1, well ahead of the document-collection experience (R20–R23). The v1 obligation is the index format plus rendering it as a nav section; summaries, snapshotting, en-masse opening and the browser extension stay deferred. One type, two jobs, arriving at different times.

## D11: References are by identity, never by position

**Date:** 2026-08-12
**Status:** decided

**Decision.** Nothing durable is addressed by byte offset or line number. Bookmarks are inline anchors that travel with the text; tags are inline markup delimiting the range they apply to; section entries reference bookmarks by name and resolve by lookup; links are ordinary markdown links.

**Why it keeps paying.** Three separate requirements had already forced this answer independently — Portal killed a bookmark side-index because it breaks whenever a range moves, D7 killed synced indexes because they go stale under hand-editing, and overlapping tags cannot be expressed positionally at all without a second structure. When three constraints select the same survivor, it is a principle rather than a preference.

**The one permitted exception is soft state.** Scroll and cursor restore (R1.2) have no anchor to attach to, since they land wherever the reader stopped. An offset within a day file is acceptable *there* precisely because being wrong is cheap and self-correcting — the reader lands slightly off and scrolls. The rule: positional addressing only where a wrong answer costs nothing.

## D12: Concurrent multi-device editing is not an expected workflow

**Date:** 2026-08-12
**Status:** decided

**Decision.** Moving between devices without an intervening sync is not an expected pattern. Concurrent divergence must therefore be **correct, visible and recoverable — not seamless.** It is a case to handle honestly, not one to optimize.

**What it deletes.** Portal's hash-based ordering rule for append-union (D51) existed to guarantee that two devices computing the same merge independently converge. With concurrent editing out of the expected path, that convergence argument does not arise, and the rule can go. Most of the merge ladder goes with it: the normal case is a fast-forward.

**What it does not delete, and this is the honest part.** The failure mode remains, it is merely rare — and "close the laptop before the push completes, then write on the phone" is a daily action whose sync state is invisible. So the requirement is a divergence that is **surfaced with a picker** rather than resolved silently, which R25 already permits as reconnection ceremony. Writes must also be atomic (write-temp-then-rename), because autosave makes interrupted writes the ordinary single-device risk — and that is the same mechanism that silently kills file-descriptor-based watchers, so directories are watched, never descriptors.

**It probably resolves Q2.** A CRDT's entire value proposition is conflict-free concurrent editing. If concurrent editing is rare and ceremony on reconnection is acceptable, that benefit is small while the cost is large — files become an export and R26 weakens. **Plain files as source of truth is the strongly indicated answer.** Recorded here as the argument; Q2 stays formally open pending confirmation.

Three good corrections, and the third one is bigger than it looks. Let me take them in order, then build the list.
Recorded: **D10** (sections and the default pin section), **D11** (references by identity), **D12** (concurrency not optimized for). `solution/features.md` is the full list with proposed stages. Q2 has been downgraded from "open" to "strongly indicated" — see below.

## You're right about pins, and for a reason I'd missed

Your model is better than mine, and the deciding argument isn't the one I was making. "Pin is a property" would need the flag stored *somewhere* — frontmatter, presumably — which means building the nav requires scanning the corpus to discover what's pinned, and the result comes back **in no particular order**. A nav panel needs an order. Membership in a distinguished fileset is one file to read, explicitly ordered, and editable by hand.

And my objection evaporates on inspection: the events calendar isn't a fileset, it's a *file entry within* one. Four entry types — bookmark, file, URL, OS-intent document — cover everything we've discussed.

The consequence worth noticing: **this gives filesets a job in v1.** The nav *is* filesets, so v1 needs the index format and the section rendering — while summaries, snapshotting, en-masse open and the browser extension stay deferred. That's the second time a type has turned out to be doing two jobs that arrive at different times, which is starting to look like a pattern worth watching for.

## Offsets: three constraints had already picked this

Agreed, and it's stronger than a preference — three separate requirements independently selected identity-based addressing. Portal killed a bookmark side-index because it breaks whenever a range moves; D7 killed synced indexes because they go stale under hand-editing; and overlapping tags can't be expressed positionally at all without a second structure. When three constraints converge on one survivor it's a principle.

The one exception I'd keep is **soft state**: scroll and cursor restore have no anchor to attach to, since they land wherever you stopped reading. An offset within a day file is fine *there* precisely because being wrong costs nothing — you land slightly off and scroll. The rule is "positional addressing only where a wrong answer is free," which is a narrow enough carve-out that it won't spread.

## The concurrency relaxation is the biggest thing in your message

It deletes more than it looks like it does. Portal's hash-based ordering rule for append-union existed *entirely* to guarantee that two devices computing the same merge independently arrive at the same bytes. If concurrent editing isn't the expected path, that convergence argument never arises and the rule goes — and most of the merge ladder with it. Normal operation is a fast-forward.

**And it probably resolves Q2.** A CRDT's whole value proposition is conflict-free concurrent editing. If that case is rare and reconnection ceremony is acceptable, you're paying a large architectural cost — plain files demoted to an export, R26 weakened, the exit made aspirational — to optimize a case that almost never happens. Plain files as source of truth looks like the answer, and I've marked Q2 "strongly indicated, needs confirming" rather than open.

The honest residual, which I don't think changes the decision but does set the bar: **"close the laptop before the push completes, then write something on the phone" is a daily action whose sync state is invisible.** So divergence has to be surfaced with a picker rather than resolved silently — which R25 already permits. Correct and visible, not seamless.

One thing the relaxation *doesn't* remove: autosave makes **interrupted writes** the ordinary single-device risk, so writes must be atomic — write-temp-then-rename. Worth flagging because that's the exact mechanism that silently kills file-descriptor-based watchers, which is one of the three findings Portal's widget work says will recur in any app that edits files a background process also touches. Watch directories, never descriptors.

## The feature list, and the five calls I'd want you to make

`solution/features.md` has everything in nine groups with a proposed stage each. Two structural notes: **"format only" is a real stage** — several things need their syntax fixed in v1 even though the feature ships later — and I've marked five assignments **◆** as genuinely arguable rather than pretending they're obvious.

| Call | My lean | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Tag a range** | v1 | This is the central structural bet. Tags are technically backfillable — the text doesn't move — but retro-tagging a year of writing is unbounded labor you'll never actually do, so "v2" means "never." |
| **Filtered view by tag** | v1 | Shares its whole mechanism with date-range views (D9), which you need anyway for "jump to a date." Nearly free once tagging exists. |
| **Substring search** | v1 | Cheap over a small corpus with no index, fixes Era 1's failure, and the app isn't livable without it within a few months. |
| **Branch a range into a file** | v2 | The real requirement is the *findable afterwards* half, and findability depends on tags and search being good first. Branching before retrieval builds the half that already worked. |
| **Rendered editing, inline constructs** | let the prototype rule | Q1's decomposition says raw+vim and rendered-read first, then rendered-edit per node type. This is exactly what the spike will tell us; assigning it now is guessing. |

One thing to say plainly: **v1 on this list is about thirty items, which is bigger than "a single-device Mac app with good editing" sounds.** Most of it is format work (cheap now, expensive later) or intrinsic to the stream, so I don't think it's creep — but it deserves a guard. I'd propose v1's own admission test, narrower than the general one: *does this serve proving the editing experience, starting the corpus durably, or making this the place the writing actually happens?* Three yeses available; anything scoring zero gets bumped.

Settle the five and I'll write the prototype spec.

I would move branching into v1, but “findable afterwards” can defer to v2 — the simple action of “take this selection, change it into its own file, update any bookmarks that exist” would be really useful in its own right. That falls under the editing experience and making it the place writing actually happens, because then I’m not perpetually worried about needing to rewrite things. Other than that, this makes good sense.

## D13: Branching a range into its own file is v1; finding it independently is v2

**Date:** 2026-08-12
**Status:** decided

**Decision.** The branch operation — take a selection, make it its own file, leave a link behind — ships in **v1**. The *independent findability* half of R14 (locating a branched file without going through its origin) waits for v2, along with tags and search.

**Why it moves up.** It scores on two of the three v1 admission tests: it is part of the editing experience, and it removes an ambient anxiety about ever needing to restructure — which is exactly the kind of friction that decides whether the tool becomes the place writing actually happens.

**Three consequences.**

- **The stream is no longer append-only.** A branch performs an interior deletion, and it can do so in a day file from months ago, so **no day file is ever final**. Portal's append-union merge degrades gracefully here by design — its prefix test fails and reconciliation falls to ordinary textual merge — and under D12 that path is rare anyway. But any later optimization that assumes historical immutability is now invalid, which is cheap to know and expensive to discover.
- **"Update any bookmarks" turns out to be a no-op**, because D11 already made anchors inline text that travels with the range. A section entry references a bookmark by name and resolves by lookup, so it finds the new location for free — provided nothing caches the resolved path. What *can* break is an ordinary markdown link pointing into the branched range, and it must break **visibly**. Portal's hardest sub-problem here — images travelling with the range, cross-repository copy-verify-delete — evaporates entirely, since Tephra is one directory rather than per-project bundles. That is the second requirement this structural choice has deleted rather than solved.
- **A branched file leaves the dated stream and therefore loses its date.** Dates come from the day-file structure (D8), and a branched file is not a day file — so it must record its **origin date in frontmatter** at branch time, or it becomes an undated object in a system organized by date. This is a format decision and therefore lands in v1 regardless of anything else.

**One thing this makes load-bearing.** With independent findability deferred, **the link left behind in the stream is v1's entire findability mechanism** for branched content. It is not a courtesy note; it is the only path back, and it should be built as a real, followable link.
EOF

# Spike 01 — experiment definition

**Answers:** Q1 (one surface, vim plus inline rendering), Q4 (stack, at the OS-integration boundary), D8 (windowed single document over day files).

This is a contract, written before building, so that "it sort of works" is not an available outcome. The artifact is disposable and will not be carried into v1.

## The decomposition that makes this cheap

The original plan was one spike answering Q1 and Q4 together. They separate, and separating them front-loads the decisive test: **the editor question can be answered in a plain browser page, at zero platform cost.** Only if it passes does the shell question matter, and only then does the windowed-document work become worth doing.

| | Question | Cost | Run if |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Does one surface do vim *and* inline widgets? | An evening | always — first |
| **A′** | Does A run acceptably on Android? | Half an hour | A passes |
| **B** | Which shell makes printing and paste cheap? | An evening or two | A passes |
| **C** | Can N day files be edited as one document? | A weekend | A passes |

**Not being spiked: candidate 1, the fully native editor.** Building vim behaviour and markdown rendering from scratch in SwiftUI/AppKit is very expensive and sits on the maintainer's weakest ground, so it is worth its cost only if A fails. This is a deliberate exclusion, not an oversight, and A failing reopens it immediately.

---

## Spike A — the editing surface

**Hypothesis.** CodeMirror 6 in a plain browser page supports a genuine vim mode *and* inline widget decorations simultaneously, with keystroke-to-paint latency imperceptible at 130 WPM in a document of realistic size.

**The sharp part is not rendering — it is vim operating over widgets.** Rendering an equation inline is well-trodden. The risk is what `dd` does to a line containing a rendered equation, whether cursor motion through a widget behaves sanely, whether visual-select spans one correctly, and whether undo puts things back. That interaction is where this either works or quietly doesn't, so it is tested explicitly rather than assumed.

**Build.** One HTML page. CodeMirror 6, vim keymap, and widget decorations for: an inline TeX equation, an inline image, and a markdown table. Load roughly 1 MB of prose so the measurement has margin. Instrument keystroke-to-paint.

**Success**, all of:
- p99 keystroke-to-paint **under 30 ms** with the document loaded, and no queueing under burst typing.
- Typing a full page at unthrottled speed **feels right** — the subjective judgement is the real criterion; the number exists to prevent talking yourself into a bad one.
- Motion across, deletion of, visual selection spanning, and undo over a rendered widget all behave the way vim should.
- Typography can be pushed to somewhere in the neighbourhood of the Clarity app's styling.

**Failure**, any of:
- Sustained p99 above 50 ms, or perceptible lag while typing.
- Vim behaviour around widgets that is wrong in a way not fixable by configuration.
- Widget rendering that degrades as the document grows.

**Not building.** Editing the rendered forms, mode switching, persistence, file loading, styling beyond what is needed to judge typography.

## Spike A′ — the same page on Android

**Hypothesis.** Spike A's page runs acceptably in Android Chrome and in a system WebView.

**Why it is here.** D4 records the sequencing's known weakness: v1's editor choice may not port to Android, and that only becomes visible in v2. This retires that risk for half an hour of work, which is an absurdly good trade.

**Build.** Serve the same page. Open it on the phone. Type into it with a Bluetooth keyboard and with the soft keyboard.

**Success.** Renders correctly, scrolls smoothly, accepts text without lag or input-method weirdness. **Failure.** Any of those failing — which would mean the desktop and mobile editors are separate builds, and that should be known now rather than in v2.

## Spike B — the OS boundary

**Hypothesis.** A native shell hosting a web view makes printing a selected range and pasting an image from the clipboard straightforward, where Tauri made them painful.

**Why these two tasks.** They are where pain has been *measured* rather than suspected, and between them they touch four requirements: printing a range (R11), pasting images in situ (R7), opening documents by OS intent (R21), and drag-and-drop later.

**Build.** The same two operations — print the current selection with a sane page setup, and paste an image from the clipboard so it lands as a file plus a markdown link — implemented twice: once in a **native Swift shell hosting a WKWebView**, once in **Electron**. Tauri needs no third implementation; its result is already known.

**Success.** Both operations work end to end, and the shell-side code for each is small enough to describe in a paragraph. Latency from Spike A is re-measured in-shell and holds.

**Failure.** Either operation requiring the kind of effort Tauri demanded, in both shells — which would mean the OS-integration cost is intrinsic rather than Tauri-specific, and would revive candidate 1 despite its price.

**Not building.** Menus, window management, app packaging, code signing, preferences.

## Spike C — the windowed document

**Hypothesis.** A window of day files can be presented as one continuous editable document (D8), with per-region write-back and stable position restore.

**Build.** Thirty synthetic day files. Load a window of them into one editor surface. Edit across a file boundary. Save. Reload and restore position.

**Success**, all of:
- Scrolling and editing show **no visible seam** at file boundaries.
- Saving touches **only the files actually edited**.
- An edit spanning a boundary is written correctly to both sides.
- Position restores to where you were, and remains correct after content is appended to an earlier file — the merge-shift case from D8.

**Failure.** A visible seam, files rewritten that were not edited, position drift on reload, or an edit spanning a boundary that corrupts or loses text.

**Not building.** The real file naming scheme, frontmatter, sync, atomic writes, tags, bookmarks.

---

## What gets recorded

Findings go to `goal/discovery/spike-01-findings.md`, and Q1 and Q4 are resolved or updated in `goal/open-questions.md` against the criteria above — as written, not as adjusted afterwards.

Let me record it, because it has three consequences worth having in writing.
**D13** recorded, `features.md` updated. Three consequences of moving branching into v1 that are worth having in writing:

**The stream stops being append-only.** A branch is an interior deletion, and it can land in a day file from months ago — so **no day file is ever final**. Portal's append-union merge handles this gracefully by design (its prefix test fails and reconciliation falls to ordinary textual merge), and under D12 that path is rare anyway. The thing to remember is negative: any later optimization assuming historical immutability is now invalid. Cheap to know, expensive to discover.

**"Update any bookmarks" turns out to be free.** D11 already made anchors inline text that travels with the range, and section entries reference them by name and resolve by lookup — so the bookmark finds its new home with no work, provided nothing caches the resolved path. What *can* break is an ordinary markdown link pointing into the branched range, and that needs to break visibly rather than silently.

Portal's hardest sub-problem here also evaporates: images travelling with the range, cross-repository copy-verify-delete, the whole apparatus. One directory instead of per-project bundles deletes it. That's now the second requirement this structure has dissolved rather than solved.

**A branched file leaves the dated stream, so it loses its date.** Dates come from the day-file structure; a branched file isn't a day file. It needs an origin date in frontmatter at branch time or it becomes an undated object in a system organized by date. That's a format decision, so it's in v1 regardless.

And one thing worth naming: with independent findability deferred, **the link left behind is v1's entire findability mechanism** for branched content. Not a courtesy note — the only path back.

## The spike, in `goal/discovery/spike-01-experiment.md`

Written as a contract, before building, so "it sort of works" isn't an available outcome.

The main idea is that the original one-big-spike plan **decomposes**, and decomposing front-loads the decisive test at nearly zero cost:

- **Spike A — the editing surface.** A plain browser page. No platform decision, no shell, no build system. An evening. What's untested is what `dd` does to a line containing a rendered equation, whether cursor motion through a widget behaves, whether visual-select spans one correctly, whether undo puts it back. Captured in `solution/architecture.md` (with the structure diagram and trust boundaries), `system-design.json`, and **D14**.

Recording it surfaced five things worth having written down, one of which I think would have bitten:

**The layering has to be loose in exactly one place.** R1.1 is a hard latency requirement, and an editing surface that routes every keystroke Z→X→W will not make it. So: **strict for operations and persistence, deliberately loose for reading live state.** The live buffer sits in memory and the editor renders straight from it; X persists asynchronously; W writes atomically. A naively pure version of this architecture violates the project's primary requirement, which is the kind of thing that gets discovered three months in when the fix is expensive.

**Document is one interface with two storage implementations** — segmented for the stream, single-file for branched documents and pinned lists. That's what makes "the notebook is one document" (D8) true in code rather than only in prose. But it's also the arrangement in which D8's split rule quietly drifts toward being size-based and runtime-chosen, so: **the rule belongs to the format spec; storage merely obeys it.**

**`branch(range)` must be a single X operation.** Create-new, update-references, delete-from-source, in that order, is the only safety mechanism available without a cross-object transaction. If Z assembles it from three primitives, the ordering guarantee is gone and the failure mode is dangling references.

**The Corpus is allowed to reach W directly for bulk scans.** Search built as "for each Document, fetch text, scan" re-reads the world. The concept lives at X, the mechanism is a directory-level scan at W — that's the layering working rather than being violated, but it has to be stated or it gets built as N calls through Document.

**X owns the quiesce protocol** — flush, release, mutate, reload — because it's the only layer that knows about both in-flight edits and files. That's dormant in v1 and load-bearing in v2, when the sync client starts mutating files under a live editor.
